messages.content: I want to enable zero-shot voice conversion across unseen tonal languages. The converted speech should carry the target speaker’s identity without changing the source speech’s lexical tone or prosody.

So the goal is to make speech sound like the target speaker while retaining what the source speaker said and how they expressed it. That includes preserving lexical tone, source intonation, and rhythm, even when the tonal language was unseen.
What does “zero-shot” add to the goal here?

It makes performance on unseen tonal languages part of the goal, rather than limiting conversion to languages already encountered. The statement does not specify a particular conversion method or what reference material, if any, is available at conversion time.
I’m trying to separate the speaker change from the things that must stay intact.

The intended change is speaker identity: the output should be accepted as belonging to the target speaker. Lexical tone and prosody are not supposed to be changed in the process. In particular, the source intonation and rhythm should be preserved.
Is lexical tone just another way of saying intonation?

No. Lexical tone concerns distinctions carried by tone in the spoken material; intonation concerns the source utterance’s broader pitch contour. Both matter here. Preserving one would not, by itself, establish that the other was preserved, and the requirement also explicitly mentions rhythm.
How precise is the lexical-tone requirement?

Lexical-tone error must remain within 2 percentage points of the error for unconverted speech. That is a comparison with the unconverted-speech baseline, not a requirement that the converted speech’s total lexical-tone error be no more than 2%.
Why say “percentage points” rather than “percent”?

Percentage points describe the absolute difference between two error rates. The requirement compares the lexical-tone error rate after conversion with the error rate for unconverted speech and allows a difference of no more than 2 percentage points. It is not phrased as a relative 2% change from the baseline.
Does that comparison replace the instruction to preserve intonation and rhythm?

No. The numerical tolerance is specifically for lexical-tone error. Preserving source intonation and rhythm remains an explicit part of the goal; the statement does not give those features a separate numerical tolerance.
And the speaker-identity side has its own number?

Yes. The target is 90% target-speaker verification acceptance at 1% false acceptance, using evaluators independent of training. That is a speaker-verification requirement, separate from the lexical-tone comparison and the instruction to preserve prosody.
Can you unpack the two percentages in that verification requirement?

The 90% figure is the required target-speaker verification acceptance. The 1% figure specifies the false-acceptance operating point at which that acceptance is evaluated. They are not two interchangeable measures of acceptance, and the requirement is not simply “90% speaker similarity.”
What is the significance of the evaluators being independent of training?

The speaker-verification result must be obtained with evaluators independent of training. The goal does not identify a particular evaluator or prescribe how one must be built; it does rule out treating a training-dependent evaluator as satisfying that stated independence condition.
If the converted voice meets the speaker-verification target but changes a lexical tone, would that still meet the goal?

A strong speaker-identity result cannot substitute for tone preservation. The lexical-tone error must still stay within 2 percentage points of unconverted speech, and the conversion is meant to preserve source intonation and rhythm rather than altering them to achieve the target voice.
What if the tones remain intact but the utterance’s rhythm changes?
That would conflict with the stated aim to preserve source rhythm. The lexical-tone error comparison addresses one part of preservation; it is not permission to change other parts of prosody.
Should I read the 90% requirement as a claim that people will identify the target speaker 90% of the time?

Not as stated. It specifies target-speaker verification acceptance at a 1% false-acceptance point, measured with evaluators independent of training. It does not separately specify a human-listener identification result.
Does this say the thresholds have already been reached?
No. These are requirements for the zero-shot voice-conversion goal, not reported experimental results. The statement sets out what the conversion should achieve across unseen tonal languages.
Could you put the full objective together without losing either the speech-preservation or speaker-identity condition?

Enable zero-shot voice conversion across unseen tonal languages that transfers the target speaker’s identity without altering lexical tone or prosody. Keep lexical-tone error within 2 percentage points of unconverted speech while preserving source intonation and rhythm, and achieve 90% target-speaker verification acceptance at 1% false acceptance using evaluators independent of training.

For the conversion approach, I propose using language-agnostic acoustic units, locking the source F0 and timing, and using reference-conditioned spectral diffusion to transfer the target speaker’s timbre.

That separates the proposed roles of the components: language-agnostic acoustic units provide a speech representation, locked source F0 and timing constrain what stays with the source utterance, and reference-conditioned spectral diffusion is intended to transfer target timbre. It is a proposed way to pursue the goal, not evidence that the preservation and speaker-verification requirements have been met.
What does “language-agnostic” mean in that description?

It describes acoustic units intended not to depend on a particular language’s labels or inventory. That fits the aim of working across unseen tonal languages, but calling the units language-agnostic does not, on its own, establish that conversion will work on those languages.
Why keep the source F0 locked?

F0 is the fundamental-frequency trajectory, a pitch-related feature of the source speech. Keeping it locked is meant to prevent target-timbre transfer from replacing that source trajectory. This is especially relevant when lexical tone and source intonation must be preserved.
Does locking F0 guarantee lexical-tone preservation?

Not by itself. It constrains an important pitch-related feature, but the proposal does not establish that every aspect relevant to lexical tone is preserved in the resulting speech. The lexical-tone error requirement still has to be assessed against unconverted speech.
And locked timing is about rhythm?

Yes. Keeping source timing locked is intended to retain the source utterance’s temporal pattern rather than letting the timbre transfer change it. That connects directly to the requirement to preserve source rhythm, although the proposal does not claim a measured rhythm-preservation result.
Where does the target speaker’s identity enter if the pitch and timing stay with the source?

In this proposal, the target reference conditions the spectral diffusion component, which is intended to transfer target timbre. The distinction is that target timbre is the intended change, while source F0 and timing are intended to remain fixed.
So the reference supplies the target voice characteristics, not new words or a new delivery?

That is the intended division of labor: use the reference to condition timbre transfer without treating it as a reason to replace the source utterance’s lexical tone, intonation, or rhythm. The proposal does not specify the reference’s format or make a claim about exactly which characteristics the system would extract from it.
What does “spectral diffusion” add to the description?

It identifies the proposed approach for generating or transforming spectral aspects of the speech under reference conditioning. Here its stated purpose is target-timbre transfer. The proposal does not specify a particular diffusion design, training procedure, or implementation.
Is target timbre the same thing as meeting the target-speaker verification requirement?

No. Transferring target timbre is the proposed means of making the converted speech carry target-speaker identity; it is not itself a verification result. The goal still calls for 90% target-speaker verification acceptance at 1% false acceptance using evaluators independent of training.
Could reference conditioning interfere with the locked source features?

The proposal assigns them different roles: the reference conditions target-timbre transfer, and source F0 and timing are locked. Whether a resulting conversion actually preserves lexical tone, intonation, and rhythm remains an open performance question, rather than something the component names alone resolve.
Does “zero-shot” here require you to specify how many target-speaker recordings the reference contains?

No number or reference format is specified in this proposal. It says the spectral diffusion is reference-conditioned and the broader goal is zero-shot conversion across unseen tonal languages. It would add an unsupported detail to infer a particular amount of reference speech.
How would you state the proposal without making it sound like a demonstrated result?

Use language-agnostic acoustic units to support conversion across unseen tonal languages, keep the source F0 and timing locked to protect its tone-related pitch trajectory and rhythm, and use reference-conditioned spectral diffusion to transfer target timbre. This describes an intended approach; it does not claim that the lexical-tone or target-speaker verification thresholds have already been achieved.
Can locking the source F0 prevent lexical-tone drift while reference-conditioned diffusion transfers timbre in unseen tonal languages?

It is a plausible constraint, but the question remains open. Locking source F0 is intended to retain the source pitch trajectory during timbre transfer. That alone does not establish that listeners or an independent assessment would find lexical tones unchanged in the converted speech, particularly across unseen tonal languages.
What exactly would F0 locking protect?

It would constrain the fundamental-frequency trajectory associated with the source utterance, rather than allowing the target reference to supply a different one. Because pitch is central to lexical tone, retaining that trajectory addresses an important route by which tone could drift. The question is whether it is sufficient when the rest of the sound is transformed.
If the F0 trajectory is locked, isn’t the lexical tone locked too?

Not necessarily. A locked F0 trajectory and preserved lexical tone are related claims, but they are not identical. The audible result still has to convey the source’s tone distinctions; fixing one specified feature does not, by definition, prove that the converted utterance does so.
Is the concern specifically the reference-conditioned diffusion step?

Yes. The question asks whether source-F0 locking can prevent drift *during* the proposed reference-conditioned timbre diffusion. The intended change is target timbre, not lexical tone. What remains uncertain is whether that transformation can leave the tone-bearing aspects of the source speech intact even with F0 constrained.
Does the target reference have to contribute pitch for the timbre transfer to work?

The proposal does not say that it does. Its stated role is to condition target-timbre transfer, while source F0 is locked. The question is not premised on deliberately importing the reference’s pitch; it asks whether unintended lexical-tone drift can still occur under that division of roles.
Would a matching F0 trace settle the question?

It would support the narrower observation that the source F0 constraint was maintained. It would not, on its own, settle whether lexical tone in the converted speech was preserved. The output’s tone must be considered as perceived or assessed in the converted speech, rather than inferred solely from the constraint.
Why emphasize unseen tonal languages in the question?

Because the question is about whether the constraint carries over beyond tonal languages encountered during development. An approach could be designed to retain source F0 without that fact alone demonstrating lexical-tone preservation across unseen tonal languages. The unseen-language condition is part of what the question asks, not a result it assumes.
Is this asking whether F0 locking helps at all, or whether it guarantees no drift?

The wording asks whether it can *prevent* lexical-tone drift. That is stronger than merely asking whether it might help. Source-F0 locking offers a reason to expect protection of the pitch trajectory, but whether it prevents drift in the resulting speech remains to be established; the question does not assert a guarantee.
How does locked timing fit into this particular question?

Locked timing is part of the broader proposed approach, but this question focuses specifically on source-F0 locking during reference-conditioned timbre diffusion. Timing concerns preservation of the source’s temporal pattern. It should not be silently treated as proof that F0 locking prevents lexical-tone drift.
Could I answer the question by saying that lexical tone depends on F0?

That explains why F0 locking is relevant, but it does not answer whether the proposed conversion prevents drift. The decisive distinction is between constraining a tone-relevant feature and establishing that the converted speech actually retains the intended lexical-tone distinctions in unseen tonal languages.
Then what would a careful answer sound like right now?

Source-F0 locking is intended to keep the source pitch trajectory in place while reference-conditioned diffusion changes timbre, so it may help protect lexical tone. Whether it *prevents* lexical-tone drift in unseen tonal languages is an open question; the proposed constraint alone does not establish that outcome.

I want to make the F0-locking question more specific. My hypothesis is that, on held-out Yoruba and Thai, F0 locking limits the increase in tone error rate to no more than 2 percentage points versus unconverted speech.

That is a testable hypothesis, not a reported outcome. It predicts that, for held-out Yoruba and Thai, tone error rate with F0 locking will be at most 2 percentage points higher than the corresponding rate for unconverted speech. It puts a numerical bound on possible tone drift rather than claiming that drift is impossible.
Does “held-out” matter to the claim, or is it just background?

It matters. The prediction is specifically about Yoruba and Thai as held-out languages. It is not merely a prediction about speech in general, and it should not be restated as though the hypothesis had already been confirmed on either language.
How does this relate to asking whether source-F0 locking can prevent lexical-tone drift during reference-conditioned timbre diffusion?

The hypothesis gives that question a particular anticipated answer: F0 locking may constrain tone error enough that any increase relative to unconverted speech is no greater than 2 percentage points on held-out Yoruba and Thai. That is narrower than claiming no lexical-tone drift whatsoever, and it remains a hypothesis about the proposed conversion setting.
Would it be accurate to call that a 2% tone error target?

No. The figure is an allowable *increase* of at most 2 percentage points over the tone error rate for unconverted speech. It does not say the total tone error rate must be 2%, and it does not describe a relative increase of 2%.
Why anchor the prediction to unconverted speech?

Unconverted speech is the stated comparison baseline. The hypothesis concerns additional tone error associated with conversion under F0 locking, so the relevant quantity is the difference from that baseline. Without the unconverted-speech rate, the stated percentage-point increase cannot be interpreted as an absolute error-rate target.
Suppose the converted speech has some tone errors. Would that automatically contradict the hypothesis?

No. The hypothesis does not require a zero tone error rate. It allows the converted-speech rate to exceed the unconverted-speech rate by up to 2 percentage points. Whether a particular observation contradicts it depends on that comparison, not simply on whether any tone errors are present.
What if the converted-speech error rate is lower than the unconverted-speech error rate?
A lower rate would not violate a hypothesis that places an upper limit on the *increase*. The wording predicts no increase greater than 2 percentage points; it does not require an increase to occur.
Does this hypothesis say that the source F0 trajectory will be perfectly reproduced?

It does not state a separate F0-trajectory accuracy result. F0 locking is the proposed constraint, and the predicted outcome here is a bound on the *tone error rate increase*. Those are related ideas, but the hypothesis should be expressed in terms of the outcome it actually names.
Could I say the hypothesis proves F0 locking is sufficient to preserve tone in unseen tonal languages?

Not at this stage. It is a prediction, not proof, and its stated scope is held-out Yoruba and Thai. Even if the predicted bound were observed, describing that result as perfect tone preservation across all unseen tonal languages would be broader than this hypothesis.
Is the bound meant to cover the target-speaker identity requirement too?

No. This hypothesis addresses tone error under F0 locking. It makes no prediction about target-speaker verification acceptance, including the separate goal of 90% acceptance at 1% false acceptance with evaluators independent of training.
What about intonation and rhythm?

They remain part of the broader preservation goal, but this hypothesis gives a numerical prediction only for tone error rate. It does not assign a measured intonation or rhythm outcome to held-out Yoruba or Thai.
Should I describe the predicted increase as being within 2 percentage points, or no greater than 2 percentage points?

“No greater than 2 percentage points” tracks the hypothesis most directly: it is an upper bound on an *increase* relative to unconverted speech. “Within 2 percentage points” can sound like a bound on differences in either direction, which is not how this particular hypothesis is worded.
Can you give me a careful one-sentence formulation?
The hypothesis is that, on held-out Yoruba and Thai, source-F0 locking during the proposed conversion limits the increase in tone error rate to ≤2 percentage points compared with unconverted speech.
To evaluate the hypothesis, I want to convert held-out Yoruba and Thai speech with F0 locked and with F0 unlocked, then independently score lexical-tone error against unconverted speech.

That sets up two conversion conditions—locked F0 and unlocked F0—for held-out Yoruba and Thai, with unconverted speech as the comparison baseline for lexical-tone error. The independent scoring would assess the converted speech rather than treating the presence of an F0 lock as proof that tone was preserved.
What does the unlocked condition tell us?

It provides a conversion condition without the F0 lock, so the lexical-tone error scores can be compared with those from the locked condition. “Unlocked” does not, by itself, specify what F0 trajectory the conversion will produce or predict which condition will have fewer tone errors.
Is unconverted speech a third conversion condition?

No. It is the baseline against which lexical-tone error is scored. The activity calls for converting the held-out speech under locked and unlocked F0 conditions, then comparing their tone error with unconverted speech.
How would this address the 2-percentage-point hypothesis?

For the locked-F0 condition, the relevant comparison is its lexical-tone error rate minus the rate for unconverted speech. The hypothesis predicts that the increase on held-out Yoruba and Thai is no greater than 2 percentage points. The activity describes how to assess that prediction; it does not report the difference.
Does the unlocked comparison change what the hypothesis predicts?

No. The ≤2-percentage-point prediction concerns the locked-F0 condition versus unconverted speech. The unlocked condition adds a comparison for examining the role of F0 locking, but the hypothesis does not assign the unlocked condition its own numerical threshold.
Could the locked condition satisfy the bound even if the unlocked condition also does?

Yes. The stated bound does not require the locked condition to outperform the unlocked one. Scoring both conditions would show how they compare, while the specific hypothesis asks whether the locked condition’s increase over unconverted speech is at most 2 percentage points.
And if locked F0 has fewer tone errors than unlocked F0, is that enough to establish the hypothesis?

Not on its own. A lower error rate than the unlocked condition is a comparison between conversion conditions. The hypothesis has a separate, absolute bound on the *increase relative to unconverted speech*: no more than 2 percentage points for the locked condition.
What is meant by scoring lexical-tone error independently?

It means the tone-error assessment should be an independent evaluation of the speech, rather than simply accepting the conversion setting or the system’s own characterization of its output. The activity does not specify a particular scoring method, scorer, or assessment protocol.
Is that the same as the independent speaker-verification evaluators in the broader goal?

They concern different assessments. Here the activity explicitly calls for independently scoring lexical-tone error against unconverted speech. The separate speaker-identity goal specifies target-speaker verification acceptance using evaluators independent of training; this activity does not say it measures speaker verification.
Why keep Yoruba and Thai held out for this activity?

The activity is intended to evaluate the prediction specifically on held-out Yoruba and Thai speech. Their held-out status is part of the stated scope; the activity does not imply that a result has already been obtained on either language.
Would observing the source F0 stayed fixed be a substitute for tone scoring?

No. Confirming the constraint would address whether F0 was locked, whereas independent lexical-tone scoring addresses the outcome the hypothesis predicts. The activity calls for scoring tone error against unconverted speech precisely because the conversion setting alone does not supply that result.
Should the tone-error comparison be described as a relative percentage change?

No. The hypothesis is expressed in percentage points: it limits the difference between the locked-conversion and unconverted-speech tone error rates to an increase of ≤2 percentage points. That is distinct from a relative percent change.
Does this activity establish that intonation, rhythm, and target-speaker identity are preserved too?

No. Its stated assessment is lexical-tone error for locked versus unlocked F0 conversion on held-out Yoruba and Thai, compared against unconverted speech. It does not specify scoring of intonation, rhythm, or target-speaker verification, so those outcomes should not be inferred from this activity.
Can you state the activity plainly, without implying that it has already succeeded?

Convert held-out Yoruba and Thai speech under locked-F0 and unlocked-F0 conditions, and independently score lexical-tone error for the converted speech against unconverted speech. The resulting scores would allow the locked-F0 condition’s increase to be checked against the hypothesized ≤2-percentage-point bound; no outcome is asserted here.

The independent annotators’ tone-error measurements are in. For Yoruba and Thai, respectively, they measured 7.4% and 9.1% on unconverted speech, 8.6% and 10.5% with F0 locked, and 13.2% and 15.0% with F0 unlocked.

Those are three measured tone-error rates for each language: an unconverted baseline and two conversion conditions. Keeping the language order consistent matters here: the first number in each pair is Yoruba, and the second is Thai.
Could you lay out the measurements by language so I don’t mix them up?

For Yoruba, independent annotators measured 7.4% tone error on unconverted speech, 8.6% with F0 locked, and 13.2% with F0 unlocked. For Thai, they measured 9.1% unconverted, 10.5% F0-locked, and 15.0% unlocked.
How much higher was tone error with F0 locked than on unconverted speech?

For Yoruba, it was 8.6% minus 7.4%, or 1.2 percentage points higher. For Thai, it was 10.5% minus 9.1%, or 1.4 percentage points higher. Those are differences in error rates, expressed in percentage points.
And what are the corresponding differences for the unlocked condition?
Unlocked tone error was 13.2% minus 7.4%, or 5.8 percentage points above unconverted speech for Yoruba. For Thai, it was 15.0% minus 9.1%, or 5.9 percentage points above unconverted speech.
Can I also compare the two converted conditions directly?

Yes. The measured unlocked rate exceeds the locked rate by 4.6 percentage points for Yoruba: 13.2% minus 8.6%. For Thai, the difference is 4.5 percentage points: 15.0% minus 10.5%. That comparison is between the two conversion conditions, not between either condition and unconverted speech.
Which set of differences uses unconverted speech as its reference?

The 1.2- and 1.4-percentage-point increases for F0-locked speech, and the 5.8- and 5.9-percentage-point increases for unlocked speech, each use the unconverted rate for the same language as their reference. The 4.6- and 4.5-percentage-point differences instead compare unlocked speech directly with F0-locked speech.
Would it be accurate to say that locked conversion produced the same tone-error rate as unconverted speech?

No. The measured rates differ: Yoruba was 7.4% unconverted and 8.6% F0-locked; Thai was 9.1% unconverted and 10.5% F0-locked. The locked rates were higher by 1.2 and 1.4 percentage points, respectively.
What does the phrase “independent annotators” establish about these numbers?

It identifies who measured the tone errors: independent annotators. The reported measurements are tone-error rates, not merely readings of the F0 setting. This evidence does not specify the annotators’ procedure or establish anything about whether a speaker-verification evaluator was independent of training.
Is the slash in “7.4%/9.1%” separating conditions?

No. It separates languages in Yoruba/Thai order. The conditions are unconverted, F0-locked, and unlocked. Thus 7.4%/9.1% gives the unconverted Yoruba and Thai rates, while 8.6%/10.5% and 13.2%/15.0% give their respective locked and unlocked rates.
Could someone read the 1.2 and 1.4 figures as relative percentage increases?

They should not. Each is an absolute difference between two percentage-valued error rates, so the unit is percentage points. For example, 8.6% minus 7.4% is 1.2 percentage points; calling it a 1.2% relative increase would express a different calculation.
Do these measurements include a result for target-speaker verification?

No. They report lexical-tone errors measured by independent annotators for Yoruba and Thai under the three stated conditions. No target-speaker verification acceptance or false-acceptance figure is reported in this evidence.
And do they directly report whether source rhythm and intonation were retained?
No. The reported outcome is tone-error rate. It does not include separate measurements of rhythm or intonation, so those properties should not be presented as measured results here.
Can you give a compact account of the evidence and its arithmetic without adding an overall verdict?

Independent annotators measured Yoruba/Thai tone-error rates of 7.4%/9.1% for unconverted speech, 8.6%/10.5% with F0 locked, and 13.2%/15.0% with F0 unlocked. Relative to unconverted speech, the F0-locked rates were higher by 1.2/1.4 percentage points and the unlocked rates by 5.8/5.9 percentage points. Directly comparing the converted conditions, unlocked rates were higher than locked rates by 4.6/4.5 percentage points.
Given the tone-error comparison, let’s retain source-F0 locking. The increases were 1.2 percentage points for Yoruba and 1.4 for Thai, versus 5.8 and 5.9 percentage points without locking.

Retain source-F0 locking. In Yoruba/Thai order, tone error increased by 1.2/1.4 percentage points with locking, compared with 5.8/5.9 percentage points without it. That comparison is the stated reason for the decision.
What are those increases measured against?

Each increase is measured against unconverted speech in the same language. The figures describe how much the tone-error rate rose after conversion, not the total tone-error rate of the converted speech.
So the 1.2 and 1.4 figures aren’t the tone-error rates themselves?
Correct. They are percentage-point differences from unconverted speech for the F0-locked condition. The 5.8 and 5.9 figures are the corresponding differences for conversion without F0 locking.
Can you keep the language order explicit when explaining the decision?
Yes. For Yoruba, the increase was 1.2 percentage points with source F0 locked versus 5.8 without locking. For Thai, it was 1.4 percentage points with locking versus 5.9 without locking.
How much smaller was the increase with locking in each language?

The increase was 4.6 percentage points smaller for Yoruba, comparing 5.8 with 1.2. It was 4.5 percentage points smaller for Thai, comparing 5.9 with 1.4. Those are differences between the reported increases, not additional tone-error measurements.
Does retaining the lock mean the converted speech had no tone errors?
No. The decision rests on a smaller *increase* in tone error with locking than without it. It does not say tone error was zero or that the F0-locked speech was identical to unconverted speech.
Am I deciding to keep source F0 specifically, rather than to lock every aspect of the source voice?
Yes. The stated decision is to retain **source-F0 locking**. It does not make a new decision about locking every other speech feature.
Does this decide how target timbre should be generated?
No new timbre-generation choice is made here. The decision is about keeping source-F0 locking in the proposed conversion approach, based on the Yoruba and Thai tone-error increases.
Could I summarize the reason as simply ‘locking performed better’?

That captures the direction of the comparison, but it loses the specific basis for the decision. A more faithful summary is that the tone-error increases relative to unconverted speech were 1.2/1.4 percentage points with locking, versus 5.8/5.9 without locking, for Yoruba/Thai.
Should I call the unlocked numbers percentage increases?

Call them **percentage-point increases** in tone-error rate. Saying only “percentage increases” could suggest a relative calculation, whereas 5.8 and 5.9 are differences between error rates measured in percent.
Does this decision establish the same outcome for every unseen tonal language?
No. Its stated numerical basis is the Yoruba and Thai comparison. Retaining the lock on that basis does not add a measured tone-error result for other languages.
And it doesn’t settle whether the target speaker’s identity transfers successfully?
Correct. The cited figures concern tone-error increases with and without source-F0 locking. This decision does not report a target-speaker verification result or a measurement of identity transfer.
What about source intonation and rhythm—are those part of this particular reason?

The reason given for this decision is the difference in measured tone-error increases. It does not report separate intonation or rhythm measurements, so retaining source-F0 locking should not be described as a demonstrated result for those properties.
Please give me a concise decision statement that includes the reason.
Retain source-F0 locking: relative to unconverted speech, Yoruba/Thai tone-error rates increased by 1.2/1.4 percentage points with locking, versus 5.8/5.9 percentage points without locking.
With source-F0 locking retained, I want to benchmark target-speaker acceptance against 90% at 1% FAR using independent verifiers, and audit Yoruba and Thai rhythm.

That is a plan for two assessments with F0 locking retained. The speaker-identity benchmark will check target-speaker acceptance against 90% at a 1% false-acceptance rate, using verifiers independent of training. The rhythm audit will examine whether the source rhythm is preserved in converted Yoruba and Thai speech. Neither outcome is reported yet.
What does FAR stand for in the benchmark?
FAR means false-acceptance rate. The plan specifies 1% FAR as the operating point for assessing target-speaker acceptance; it is not a second target-speaker acceptance figure.
So am I asking whether acceptance reaches 90% while false acceptance is set at 1%?

Yes. The benchmark asks whether target-speaker verification acceptance reaches 90% at the 1% FAR operating point. Reporting an acceptance figure without its associated FAR would not fully express the stated benchmark.
What role do the independent verifiers play?
They provide the target-speaker verification assessment independently of training, as required by the broader goal. The plan does not name particular verifiers or prescribe their design.
Would a judgment from the conversion system itself serve the same purpose?

It would not, by itself, meet the plan’s call for independent verifiers. The benchmark is meant to assess target-speaker acceptance through verifiers independent of training, rather than treat the conversion system’s own output or characterization as the verification result.
Does this plan change the choice to keep source F0 locked?
No. It takes retained source-F0 locking as the setting for the planned benchmark and rhythm audit. It does not propose another locked-versus-unlocked comparison or a new F0 decision.
Why check speaker acceptance when F0 is locked?

The conversion is intended to transfer target-speaker identity while keeping source F0 constrained. Benchmarking acceptance in that setting checks the speaker-identity requirement directly; retaining the F0 lock does not, on its own, establish that verifiers will accept the output as the target speaker.
Is the 90% figure about how often the voice sounds similar to the target to a listener?

The stated measure is target-speaker *verification acceptance* at 1% FAR using independent verifiers. The plan does not specify a separate listener-similarity judgment, so it would be more precise to keep the verification wording.
What exactly is covered by the Yoruba and Thai rhythm audit?

It is an audit of rhythm in the Yoruba and Thai conversion setting, in light of the goal to preserve source rhythm. The plan does not specify a rhythm metric, a numerical tolerance, or a particular audit procedure.
Does mentioning Yoruba and Thai mean the rhythm audit covers every unseen tonal language?
No. Yoruba and Thai are the languages explicitly named for this audit. The plan does not extend that rhythm audit to every unseen tonal language or state what its findings will be.
Does a rhythm audit also establish that source intonation is preserved?

No. Rhythm and intonation are distinct aspects of prosody. The broader goal includes preserving both, but this plan specifically calls for an audit of Yoruba and Thai rhythm; it does not state a separate intonation audit or result.
Could successful target-speaker verification stand in for the rhythm audit?

No. Verification acceptance addresses whether the speech is accepted as the target speaker at the specified FAR. The rhythm audit addresses preservation of the source utterance’s rhythm. The plan includes both because they answer different questions.
And would the rhythm audit tell us whether the 90% verification target was reached?
No. An assessment of source rhythm would not supply target-speaker verification acceptance. That figure has to come from the planned benchmark using independent verifiers at 1% FAR.
Are there any numerical pass criteria for rhythm in this plan?

None are stated. The plan says to audit Yoruba and Thai rhythm, while the explicit numerical benchmark here is 90% target-speaker acceptance at 1% FAR. Adding a rhythm threshold would go beyond the plan.
Should I describe the 90% benchmark as already satisfied because it is in the plan?
No. Ninety percent is the value to benchmark against, not an observed acceptance rate. The plan calls for the measurement with independent verifiers; it does not provide its result.
Can you restate the plan in one sentence without implying that either assessment is complete?

With source-F0 locking retained, benchmark target-speaker verification acceptance against 90% at 1% FAR using verifiers independent of training, and audit preservation of source rhythm in Yoruba and Thai speech.
For the speaker-acceptance benchmark, I’ll run frozen ECAPA-TDNN and ResNet speaker verifiers on converted Yoruba and Thai utterances. I’ll calibrate each verifier at 1% FAR on disjoint speakers.

That specifies two speaker verifiers and a separate calibration for each. Both ECAPA-TDNN and ResNet will be run on the converted Yoruba and Thai utterances, with each calibrated to a 1% false-acceptance rate using disjoint speakers. This describes the assessment activity, not its acceptance results.
